newsitem.title: USA: "People's Summit" protests welfare cuts, unemployment.
newsitem.headline: "People's Summit" protests welfare cuts, unemployment.

text.p: While President Clinton and other dignitaries promoted volunteerism Monday, protesters at an alternative "People's Summit" said government, not volunteers, must ensure jobs and health care for the poor.

"We're here to say that not all is well in America. Some of us aren't getting basic justice, and that's more important than volunteering," said Sister Margaret McKenna, a Roman Catholic nun who joined the crowd of several hundred labour union members and social activists at the alternative rally.

Among speakers to the crowd were two -- Philadelphia Mayor Ed Rendell and Rev. Jesse Jackson -- who had earlier addressed Independence Hall ceremonies of the official presidents' summit on volunteerism, which ends Tuesday.

"As mayor of the host city, I got to speak at the summit, and I told them that I endorsed some of the goals of the summit ... because I think there is a place for volunteerism," Rendell told the alternative rally.

"But I also told them that you were meeting here ... and I told them that you were right. Because unless we do something about poverty and jobs for people, that this city and every other city is in trouble, and trouble that all the volunteers in the world won't fix," Rendell said.

Rendell said cuts in government welfare programmes, passed last year, would increase the number of job seekers in the city by between 40,000 and 70,000 by the year 2000. That is in addition to 48,000 now looking for work and numerous others who have given up.
He told protesters to urge Congress to pass a "meaningful" jobs bill to help absorb people being cut off welfare.

Others were more critical of the official summit, which began Sunday with Clinton, retired Gen. Colin Powell, former presidents and thousands of others painting over graffiti and cleaning up an eight-mile stretch of Philadelphia street.
Henry Nicholas, the main organiser of the protest, called the volunteer summit a "Hollywood-type photo-op."

"We could not let the presidents who have presided over decades of failed policy come and give us a paint job," Nicholas, president of the National Union of Hospital and Health Care Employees, told Reuters.
"If you wanted to help youth, then you should create jobs so their mothers and fathers can go to work and they can have a proper role model," he said.
Many of those attending the rally were active volunteers.

Cheri Honkala, director of the Kensington Welfare Rights Union, a Philadelphia group, said: "We're not against volunteering, because we volunteer every day of our lives. But I think that what we're interested in is talking about issues of homelessness, of poverty, of unemployment, and some of the things that are not being addressed ... at the president's summit."
